rationale: The hypothesis posits that nystagmus (HP:0000639) is a core neuro-ophthalmological feature found across both the mild (childhood-onset) and severe (infantile/neonatal-onset) ends of the NKX6-2-related disorder spectrum, rather than being restricted to cases with diffuse hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. This is directly corroborated by the comprehensive phenotypic descriptions in GeneReviews (Chelban et al., 2018) and cohort studies (Chelban et al., 2017, 2020; Baldi et al., 2018; Bereshneh et al., 2020). GeneReviews explicitly documents nystagmus as a hallmark feature at both extremes: presenting as 'neonatal-onset nystagmus' in the severe, rapidly progressive infantile form, and as a cerebellar finding ('nystagmus, extraocular movement disorder, dysarthria, titubation, and ataxia') in the milder, childhood-onset complex spastic ataxia form. Furthermore, Chelban et al. (2020) demonstrated that NKX6-2 phenotypes can occur even in the absence of overt hypomyelination, while nystagmus and cerebellar ataxia remain central clinical hallmarks. No counter-evidence in the available literature indicates that nystagmus is selectively restricted only to diffuse hypomyelinating cases.

evidence.text: GeneReviews explicitly characterizes nystagmus across both severity spectra: presenting as neonatal-onset nystagmus at the severe end, and as part of the cerebellar findings (nystagmus, extraocular movement disorder, dysarthria, titubation, and ataxia) in the milder childhood-onset complex spastic ataxia presentation.

source.title: NKX6-2-related disorder
source.quote: At the severe end of the spectrum is neonatal-onset nystagmus, severe spastic tetraplegia with joint contractures and scoliosis... At the milder end of the spectrum is normal achievement of early motor milestones in the first year of life followed by slowly progressive complex spastic ataxia with pyramidal findings... and cerebellar findings (nystagmus, extraocular movement disorder, dysarthria, titubation, and ataxia)

numbers.metric: total reported individuals across families in review

evidence.text: Chelban et al. (2020) evaluated an expanded cohort of 11 new cases from 8 families alongside previously published cases, showing a phenotypic spectrum ranging from neonatal onset with worse prognosis to milder childhood onset with predominantly motor involvement. They note that NKX6-2 variants can cause disease in the absence of overt hypomyelination and highlight nystagmus and cerebellar ataxia as hallmark features.

source.title: Genetic and phenotypic characterization of NKX6‐2‐related spastic ataxia and hypomyelination
source.quote: Our data reveal a phenotype spectrum with neonatal onset, global psychomotor delay and worse prognosis at the severe end and a childhood onset with mainly motor phenotype at the milder end. The phenotypic and neuroimaging expression in NKX6-2 is described and it is shown that phenotypes with epilepsy in the absence of overt hypomyelination and diffuse hypomyelination without seizures can occur. Conclusions: NKX6-2 mutations should be considered in patients with autosomal recessive, very early onset of nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia with hypotonia that rapidly progresses to spasticity

evidence.text: The discovery study by Chelban et al. (2017) identified 7 affected individuals across 3 families. Two families showed childhood onset with slow progression (patients surviving into their 30s and 40s) with predominant ataxia, whereas the third family exhibited earlier onset associated with hypomyelination, with neonatal presentation including hypotonia and nystagmus.

source.title: Mutations in NKX6-2 cause progressive spastic ataxia and hypomyelination
source.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
source.quote: Affected individuals can present as neonates with severe hypotonia and nystagmus or later with progressive spasticity and ataxia.

evidence.text: Baldi et al. (2018) reported 10 patients with homozygous NKX6-2 variants who shared psychomotor delay, spastic quadriparesis, hypotonia, and nystagmus, confirming nystagmus as a core feature of the presentation, while finding no clear genotype-phenotype correlation cleanly separating findings.

source.title: Expanding the clinical and genetic spectra of NKX6‐2‐related disorder
source.quote: Our patients share a primary diagnosis of psychomotor delay, and they show spastic quadriparesis, nystagmus and hypotonia.

evidence.text: Bereshneh et al. (2020) identified two siblings with a homozygous missense variant presenting with horizontal and vertical nystagmus alongside oculomotor apraxia, developmental delay, spasticity, and peripheral axonal neuropathy, with cerebellar white matter involvement.

source.title: Expanding the clinical and neuroimaging features of NKX6-2-related hereditary spastic ataxia type 8
source.quote: spasticity and contracture, scoliosis, hip dislocation, oculomotor apraxia, horizontal and vertical nystagmus. In addition, wrist and foot drop due to peripheral axonal neuropathy were observed

new_directions.question_text: What specific subtypes of nystagmus (e.g., pendular, gaze-evoked, upbeat/downbeat, or periodic alternating) distinguish the early infantile presentation from the childhood-onset cerebellar ataxia presentation?
new_directions.rationale: While nystagmus is documented in both severe/infantile and milder/childhood presentations, electro-oculography or detailed neuro-ophthalmic taxonomy is infrequently detailed across reports. Determining whether pendular sensory nystagmus predominates in early dysmyelinating cases versus gaze-evoked cerebellar nystagmus in later-onset ataxia cases could provide greater discriminating power.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact incidence of absent nystagmus in proven biallelic NKX6-2 patients, and does absence correlate with particular missense mutations outside the homeobox domain?
new_directions.rationale: Quantifying the negative predictive value of absent nystagmus across international multi-center cohorts will clarify whether absence of nystagmus strongly excludes NKX6-2 disease.
